item.title: A Bernstein-Type Variance-Adaptive PMW Mechanism for DP Query Release
item.description: arXiv:2611.33045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Private Multiplicative Weights (PMW) is a central mechanism for the differentially private release of adaptive linear statistics over a finite universe. Its classical analysis uses a fixed multiplicative-weights learning rate and does not exploit the local variance of the current hypothesis. This paper presents PMW-Bernstein, a variance-adaptive refinement in which the update step is determined by the relationship between the privately estimated query error and the variance under the current hypothesis. The mechanism retains the standard PMW privacy architecture based on Sparse Vector screening, Gaussian numerical measurements, sequential composition, and post-processing. Through a potential-based analysis, we prove a one-step progress bound that yields a global weighted energy bound, recovers the classical $O(1/{\alpha}2)$ update regime in general, and establishes an $O(1/{\alpha})$ update regime under a Bernsteintype condition on updated rounds. Controlled simulations over synthetic finite-universe distributions and query workloads show that the adaptive rule reduces the number of updates in the low-variance regime, remains competitive in the high-variance regime, and succeeds within the prescribed update budget in the heterogeneous regime where the fixed-step baseline fails.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Aniss Benstaali, Habib Louafi, Naima Bessah

item.title: The Date You Didn't Set: The System-Prompt Date as a Hidden Variable in LLM Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2611.31254v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The system prompt of many instruction-tuned models carries a date, usually today's, filled in automatically for conversational and agentic requests alike, so an unchanged evaluation can send a different prompt each day. In this paper, we explore how much this hidden input changes evaluation outcomes. Across six instruction-tuned models and four benchmarks, with prompts, decoding, and configuration fixed, every model is affected: two plausible dates (2024--2026) switch a median $6.6\%$ of test items between correct and incorrect. Even rerunning the evaluation one day later flips about as many items as changing the batch size, although nothing in the setup was changed. In addition, using a grammar-constrained variant of Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) to search dates of any year, we find dates that cost the Llama-3.x models up to $36.5$ points of held-out accuracy. Beyond accuracy, switching to another plausible date alters LLM-judge verdicts and undoes $15$--$32\%$ of reproduced jailbreak successes on Llama-3.2-3B. Yet none of the eleven evaluation stacks we audit pins the date. With the date and the rest of the setup fixed, reruns reproduce byte-for-byte; we therefore recommend pinning, logging, and reporting the date.
item.dc:creator: Noureldin Zahran, Mohammed E. Fouda, Khaled N. Khasawneh

item.title: PEACE-TEST-PROTOCOL: Polarization-Keyed Examination Papers and Mandatory Issued Eyewear that Displace AI Glasses and Extend Universal Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.31299v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Camera-equipped AI glasses turn an examination page into a query for a remote vision-language model. Device detection targets possession, and our companion work SEOYUN targets the model. PEACE-TEST-PROTOCOL instead changes who owns the eyewear. Every candidate wears authority-issued glasses for the whole session, and the question paper is printed so that it can be read only through them. As in cinema stereoscopy, a patterned laminate encodes the text in the handedness of circular polarization rather than in brightness. The page looks uniformly grey to the naked eye and to unfiltered cameras, and the issued circular analyzer reveals the text. Compulsory issued eyewear turns the smart-glasses form factor against itself. The face position is occupied by a device the authority supplies and collects, and a camera anywhere else needs its own analyzer. Spectacle wearers receive prescription inserts in the issued frame, low-vision candidates may use an offline assistive mixed-reality tier, and blind candidates keep braille, audio, and screen-reader formats. We derive the luminance and contrast budget and show why circular keying tolerates head tilt. A simulation study supports the analysis. A spectral Mueller model confirms tilt invariance and invisibility to linear-polarization cameras, but a 1 degree axis misregistration leaks a few percent of contrast. A capture-and-OCR experiment on English and Korean text shows that video averaging can recover leakage too weak to read in a single frame, so leakage must be bounded against the adversary's total photon budget. Data from 151 observers and 28 cameras show that spectral (metameric) keys are visible to all of them. The key carries no secrecy, and filtered covert cameras remain possible. All results are simulations; no prototypes, physical measurements, or human-subject results are reported.
item.dc:creator: Dohyeon Kwon

item.title: When Successful Collaboration Becomes an Attack Surface: Insider Memory Poisoning in Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.31307v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) increasingly use shared memory to store and reuse successful collaboration records, enabling teams to improve across tasks. However, this memory introduces a new attack surface for malicious insiders. Unlike existing insider attacks that inject misleading information directly into the current collaboration, misinformation stored in shared memory can later appear as successful team experience and gain greater credibility and influence. We propose MIMPA (Multi-Agent Insider Memory Poisoning Attack), which exploits this vulnerability using only normal participation privileges, without direct memory access. During an earlier task, the malicious agent embeds a target-specific payload while helping the team answer correctly, allowing the payload to be retained in a successful collaboration record. When retrieved for a later target task, this poisoned record can steer benign agents toward a designated wrong answer, further amplified by malicious triggering. Across three benchmarks and two LLM backbones, MIMPA substantially outperforms existing insider attacks and remains effective under hierarchical memory management, while auditing only partially mitigates it. These results reveal that shared memory intended to accumulate team experience can become a persistent channel for insider attacks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ahnji0520/MIMPA-code.
item.dc:creator: Jihyung Ahn, Buru Chang

item.title: Pearl: TEE-Enabled Fair Ordering with Minimal Replication
item.description: arXiv:2611.31468v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent research has investigated fair transaction ordering in blockchain consensus. An orthogonal line of work has demonstrated that equipping replicas with trusted execution environments (TEEs) enables more efficient consensus protocols with only $2f{+}1$ replicas. In this work, we bridge these two areas and demonstrate that two key fair-ordering properties, ordering linearizability and $\gamma$-batch-order fairness with minimal batching, cannot be implemented in partially synchronous networks with $2f{+}1$ replicas, even when the replicas are equipped with TEEs. We show that Byzantine replicas can circumvent TEE protections by manipulating the timing of transaction submissions to the enclave, thereby biasing the resulting ordering indicators. However, we prove that assuming a synchronous network allows both properties to be implemented with a reduced replica count. We propose two mechanisms: one uses absolute TEE-attested timestamps to guarantee ordering linearizability in a system of $n \ge 2f{+}1$ replicas, and the other uses TEE-maintained relative sequence numbers to guarantee $\gamma$-batch-order fairness when $n > \frac{2\gamma f}{2\gamma-1}$. Ultimately, we integrate these mechanisms into a synchronous lane-based consensus algorithm, achieving strong fair-ordering properties and superior performance while requiring fewer replicas than representative state-of-the-art baselines.
item.dc:creator: Vian Robotin, J\'er\'emie Decouchant, Shaokang Xie, Dakai Kang, Mohammad Sadoghi

item.title: How Small Can a Single Shor Run Be? Limits and Constructions for secp256k1
item.description: arXiv:2611.31585v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Most resource estimates for breaking secp256k1 with Shor's algorithm describe one long run per attempt, and the spacetime volume of that run, its peak number of logical qubits times its Toffoli count, sets its logical-error budget. Eker{\aa}'s tradeoff shrinks each run by using more runs, but how far it can shrink the largest run, and at what circuit cost, has not been determined. We minimize the volume of the largest run while every key is recovered with probability at least 0.99, within ten times the total volume of three runs of H\"aner et al.\ and $2^{40}$ classical operations. We prove that a linear run fixed in advance, which starts its group register at a point and discards its label, reveals at most $\log_2(1+(|S|-1)/r)$ bits about a uniform key, where $|S|$ counts its exponent values and $r$ is the group order. With generic post-processing and the baseline's window costs, splitting alone then shrinks the largest run at most 1.86 times within the budget. To gain more, we make each exponent bit cheaper with windows that share one table point among exponent values related by six symmetries of the curve, on a point-addition core borrowed from the ECDSA.Fail leaderboard. One random scalar and one random start per run give every approximate addition uniform operands, and a bound on each run's outcomes certifies, for every key, a decoder that discards flagged runs. We count every Toffoli gate and every qubit of every run, and each configuration solved all 563 of its pre-registered simulated trials on secp256k1. The best one shrinks the largest run 3.87 times at 8.79 times the baseline's total volume, against 2.81 times for Eker{\aa}'s tradeoff on the same core, and its run is at least 2.6 times smaller than every design of Initio Intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Yicheng Guang, Yuliang Xiong, Yueqi Chen, Xun Gao

item.title: Your bids are showing: re-identifying power plants in anonymized market data, and a differentially private alternative
item.description: arXiv:2611.31681v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: ERCOT publishes every generator's hourly offer curve 60 days after the operating day. Market monitors, researchers and traders use these records to study the merit order and check for withholding. PJM publishes the same kind of data with unit names replaced by codes, on the view that masking keeps offers confidential. We test that view on ERCOT data from 2024 to 2026, where names are public and so provide ground truth, by masking the records under PJM's published rules. Public EIA and EPA data match 25% of the masked units we can score (32% of their capacity) to their plant, and 45% fall within the top five guesses. PJM's feed carries the same fields, so we expect masking to fail there too. Publishing exact fuel-group totals instead does not help. An attacker who knows the other units in a group recovers one unit's high-price offers exactly, and an outsider who knows only the target's outage dates reaches a correlation of 0.77, most of it from a few renewable and hydro units that offer at very high prices (0.32 over fossil units). We propose a differentially private release: monthly totals by fuel group and price bin, with Gaussian noise calibrated under zero-concentrated differential privacy so that each unit's whole year of offers is protected. It publishes an unbiased noisy layer and derives a monotone supply curve and shares from it at no extra privacy cost. At $\varepsilon=10$ per unit-year the market supply curve stays within 11% of the truth, the implied clearing price within \$3.0/MWh, and the attacker's correlation falls to 0.23. Whether an analysis still works depends on one ratio, how much the true quantity varies month to month against the noise, which predicts the accuracy of totals to within 0.05. The clearing price, supply slope and combined-cycle capacity remain usable, but no monthly release, private or exact, can answer questions about single hours or single units.
item.dc:creator: Nikhil Ravi

item.title: TACT-Bench: Testing Adaptive Conversational Threats against Tool-Use Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.31756v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The growing autonomy of AI agents in using external tools and making decisions has created an urgent need for comprehensive safety benchmarks. Existing benchmarks test compromised tool channels or adaptive multi-turn attacks, though they may not capture the unique capabilities of policy-governed tool-use agents, which must resist unauthorized requests without abandoning the legitimate work embedded in the same interaction. To fill this gap, we introduce TACT-Bench, a stateful benchmark built around scenario-specific stories, personas, manipulation tactics, and response-adaptive escalation. Each adversarial task targets an action explicitly prohibited by the policy provided to the assistant, while the policy remains hidden from the attacking user. TACT pairs each adversarial task with at least one benign counterpart, and its adversarial tasks retain authorized ground-truth actions when a compliant resolution remains available. We define these base tasks as TACT-Base. We additionally introduce TACT-TrustPrime, which places an independent benign task before an unrelated attack in the same conversation. We also propose Paired Selective Trustworthiness (PST), which combines explicit safe refusal with demonstrated capability on matched benign tasks, to analyze an agent's overcautiousness and practicality. Averaged across 6 different models as assistants, TACT-Base raises Attack-Induced Failure Rate (AFR) by 17.53% over four compatible attack baselines, and TACT-TrustPrime raises it by a further 17.01%. The two evaluated defense methods reduce AFR by only 8.35%--9.41% on average and do not consistently improve PST, underscoring the need for stronger policy-enforcement methods.
item.dc:creator: Ilia Hashemi Rad, Feijie Wu, Haoyu Wang, Jing Gao

item.title: BODYBENCH: Evaluating Adversarial Image Defenses Against AI Nudification Inpainting
item.description: arXiv:2611.31774v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Adversarial perturbation defenses protect images from unauthorized edits by adding imperceptible noise. Yet none of these methods have been evaluated against nudification, despite AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII) being among the most documented harms of generative AI. Moreover, nudification edits are readily carried out through inpainting, the primary setting these protection methods are designed to defend against. We argue this is a problem-formulation failure since prior threat models do not correspond to nudification edits (also called attacks). The misalignment of existing approaches is structural, spanning mask shape, training and testing prompt distributions, and success criterion which causes existing evaluations to systematically overestimate protection effectiveness. We reformulate image protection against unauthorized editing around this documented harm. We introduce BODYBENCH, a benchmark of 648 fully synthetic clothed adult subjects, each paired with 11 mask variants spanning body, face, and context regions. We propose three harm-aligned metrics: sexualization, naturalness, and recognizability that jointly determine whether an inpainted output constitutes a successful nudification attack. Auditing four recent protection methods (PhotoGuard, DiffusionGuard, AdvPaint, DiffVax) on BODYBENCH, we find that protection succeeds in only one configuration of one method, and only under exact mask alignment between defender and attacker---a condition no real defender can guarantee and one that we show is easily always bypassed. We also show that standard evaluation metrics such as peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) are essentially uncorrelated with nudification protection. BODYBENCH makes this misalignment measurable and provides a foundation for defenses grounded in documented harm.
item.dc:creator: Li Qiwei, Salma Abdel Magid, Olga Russakovsky, Eric Gilbert, Sarita Schoenebeck

item.title: Audits Need Access, Data, and Compute. But How Much?
item.description: arXiv:2611.31968v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI audits have garnered significant attention in recent months, as the ability to test and monitor AI models plays a crucial role in safe development and deployment. However, AI audit success hinges on an auditor's authority; in particular, what information and resources they have at their disposal. Ongoing debates have surrounded the question: How much model access is needed to conduct an AI audit? Auditors seek more model access, while companies resist it for reasons related to confidential business information (trade secrets) and privacy. This tug-of-war remains unresolved. Further, this debate misses a related question: How much data and compute do auditors need? In this work, we systematically investigate both questions. We provide a framework that varies each of these three dimensions-model access, data, and compute-and measures their joint effect on audit success. We apply this framework to three tasks. We find that (1) some model access is important, but there can be diminishing returns; (2) data and compute matter more for traditional fairness audits, but model access matters more for manipulation and lie detection; and (3) these three resources can be fungible (i.e., an exchange rate exists between them), meaning that model access is not the only salient factor. These results suggest that audit governance should jointly consider different dimensions of auditor authority (including model access, data, and compute) in relation to audit objectives. These issues are particularly salient as we consider the spectrum of auditing setups, from a small ecosystem of embedded evaluators with significant access to a large body of third-party auditors with greater independence but limited access. Our framework serves as a template that can be applied to different audit tasks and inform the degree of auditor authority.
item.dc:creator: Salil Goyal, Sarah H. Cen, Daniel E. Ho

item.title: Online Environment Repair for Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.32037v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Programmatic verifiers provide scalable reward signals for training coding agents with reinforcement learning, yet subtle harness defects and incomplete unit tests allow policies to earn full credit without solving the intended task. Existing training-time defenses intervene either by penalizing suspicious outputs or by filtering flagged tasks and rollouts. However, output penalties leave the underlying verifier exploitable, driving policies to disguise shortcuts under reasoning monitors or zeroing out valid solutions under detector false positives, whereas task and rollout filtering discards or mutes the hardest problems where shortcuts emerge earliest. Pre-training verifier hardening repairs the environment directly, but misses vulnerability classes that surface only as the policy improves during reinforcement learning. In this paper, we propose online environment repair, which leaves triggering rollout rewards unchanged to remove hiding incentives and asynchronously patches exploited environments during training. Candidate repairs triggered by execution invariants or differential fuzzing are deployed only after passing three automated validation gates that block the exploit while preserving valid solutions, canceling detector false positives and enabling structural propagation across repositories without scaffold labels or reference solutions. Across 20 controlled GRPO experiments on heterogeneous software-engineering repositories, online environment repair reduces cumulative reward hacking from 36.9% to 0.06% and improves held-out Pass@8 from 21.7% to 46.7%, consistently outperforming reward-penalty, rollout-filtering, and static-hardening baselines while eliminating zero-shot exploitation on unseen loophole classes.
item.dc:creator: Sheng Lu, Rui Mao, Zewei Chen, Chihua Ying, Beiduo Chen, Dingxin Hu, Tinghao Yu

item.title: Query-Guided Visual Minimization for Selective Disclosure to Cloud VLMs
item.description: arXiv:2611.32302v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cloud-hosted vision-language models (VLMs) require sending images beyond the user's local trust boundary, potentially exposing sensitive information the query does not need. We study query-guided visual minimization: a trusted local transformation preserves query-relevant visual content and reduces unnecessary disclosure before transmission. Unlike query-agnostic anonymization, it preserves the same sensitive content when the query requires it and suppresses it otherwise. We introduce QGVM, a framework that combines query grounding with an independent sensitive-item inventory, determines disclosure necessity at the type, instance, and text-content levels, and renders a minimized image for a black-box downstream VLM. We evaluate QGVM on complementary benchmarks measuring task utility, directly recoverable sensitive information, and inferential geolocation leakage. With OpenAI GPT-6.1 Sol, QGVM achieves 85.3% DoxBench answer correctness versus 77.5% for PGP, while a separately prompted Sol geolocation attacker succeeds within 1 km on 5.8% of QGVM images versus 25.7% of unprotected images. On Scene-Privacy, QGVM reduces face re-identification from 27.7% (PGP) to 4.5%. On held-out BIV-Priv-Seg, unnecessary private-text recovery falls from 33.9% (PGP) to 15.3%. To verify that disclosure is query-dependent, we evaluate paired queries that either require or do not require the same sensitive information. QGVM achieves 69.6% correct disclosure switching, compared with 29.1% for grounding-only cropping. These findings highlight the value of distinguishing visual relevance from disclosure necessity, while revealing the privacy-utility trade-offs of selective visual disclosure.
item.dc:creator: Pedram Zaree, Kleomenis Katevas, Vandana Rajan, Nael Abu-Ghazaleh, Hamed Haddadi

item.title: ArabFake: A multitask deep learning framework for Arabic fake news Detection, Categorization, and risk prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.32303v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The spread of fake news among Arabic media including social media represents a great challenge to the integrity of information and the trust of the public in it. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive deep-learning framework, named ArabFake, that goes beyond the binary classification on Arabic fake news detection. ArabFake, built over MARBERTv2 (a state-of-the-art model for multi-dialectal Arabic tweets), proficiently address the complexity of the Arabic language while performing three unified tasks which are fake news detection, content categorization and its risk assessment. The framework promotes efficiency and performance both by enabling multi-task learning through shared knowledge representation across tasks. In order to facilitate development and evaluation, we present the ArabFake Dataset consisting of 2,495 manually labelled news items with labels that are verified by experts regarding fake news categories and risk levels. ArabFake demonstrates robust performance, achieving an F1 score of 94.12% for fake news detection, 84.92% for categorization, and 88.91% for risk zone assessment, highlighting its reliability and effectiveness across multiple tasks. We improve interpretability and extract insight into manipulative techniques by integrating valence scoring as part of the framework that emphasizes misleading linguistic cues used to disseminate fake news within the produced image. The results show that ArabFake is a holistic Arabic fake news detection framework that has practical implications on news organizations and fact checking projects.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Maher Khafaga Shehata, Mohammed Nasser Al-Suqri, Nour Eldin Mohamed Elshaiekh Osman, Faten Hamad, Yousuf Nasser Alhusaini, Ahmed Mahfouz

item.title: On the solving degree and complexity of Gr\"obner Basis computation over finite fields
item.description: arXiv:2611.32456v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Solving systems of multivariate polynomial equations over finite fields is a central problem in algebraic cryptanalysis, commonly approached using Gr\"obner basis algorithms. The complexity of Gr\"obner basis computation depends on the algorithm employed and is governed by the solving degree, defined as the maximum degree of the polynomials processed during the computation. Estimating this quantity is therefore crucial, and several bounds in terms of the degree of regularity have been established in the literature. In this work, we investigate the effect of Buchberger's criteria on the elimination of redundant pairs, and prove that the solving degree of a Gr\"obner basis algorithm combining linear algebra with Buchberger's original algorithm is bounded above by the degree of regularity defined by the leading forms of the involved polynomials. This result provides a rigorous justification for using the degree of regularity in complexity estimates for Gr\"obner basis algorithms, thereby supporting a common assumption in algebraic cryptanalysis. We refine the complexity analysis by establishing bounds on the number of pairs that must be processed. These bounds improve upon published complexity estimates, with particularly significant gains in certain parameter ranges.
item.dc:creator: Irene Di Muzio, Igor Semaev

item.title: CAPTA: Identifying LLMs Behind AI Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.32686v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents access remote services through tools to complete user tasks, often via API calls. In this setting, a remote service may want to identify the backend LLM of an agent to launch model-specific attacks, including prompt injection or selective delivery of manipulated content. However, the service cannot directly query the backend model and must instead collect observable responses through its interactions with the agent, making identification challenging. In this paper, we present Completely Automated Preference Test to tell LLMs Apart (CAPTA), a model identification approach inspired by CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart), which distinguishes humans from automated programs. CAPTA presents multiple-choice questions as verification challenges, using differences in models' selection preferences to identify the backend LLM. It selects questions based on cross-model option-generation diversity and uses LLM-guided search to optimize their option sets. Our evaluation shows that CAPTA achieves 99.0% mean identification accuracy with only 10 questions across 25 LLMs from 10 model families. We further evaluate CAPTA with four widely used agents and seven representative LLMs, achieving 99.7% mean identification accuracy across all 28 agent-LLM combinations with 30 submitted answers.
item.dc:creator: Kailun Yan, Yue Huang, Sisi Duan

item.title: Red-Teaming a Sovereign LLM, Its Reasoning and Its Training Stages
item.description: arXiv:2611.32710v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for applications with sensitive information. We investigate whether confidentiality instructions in system prompt can protect such information. We red-team Apertus v1.5, an open sovereign LLM, and five other model families across six languages and reasoning modes. We use synthetic personal records to evaluate direct disclosure, correction baits, yes/no verification, derived-value queries, reasoning leakage and authorisation checks. We also explore copyright attribution, historical misrepresentation and stereotyping. Despite confidentiality instructions, Apertus 8B and 70B leak information in 96% and 95% of requests, respectively, in correction-bait attacks. Verification and derived-value queries also expose protected information without necessarily revealing identifiers. Moreover, reasoning traces can leak confidential records even when final answers withhold them. Our experiments also show that post-training does not consistently improve safety. Our findings demonstrate that system prompts alone cannot ensure confidentiality and highlight the need for multilingual reasoning-aware safety evaluations.
item.dc:creator: Hatef Otroshi Shahreza

item.title: Sound Distributed Runtime Verification under Incomplete Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2611.32868v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Distributed runtime verification often requires combining evidence from several nodes to check properties that cannot be evaluated locally. However, when messages are delayed, lost, or deliberately suppressed, the verifier may not know whether a violation occurred or whether the relevant evidence is missing. This creates a risk of incorrectly reporting compliance. We study the requirements for sound monitoring under these conditions. We first show that a deadline-bounded monitor cannot be simultaneously sound, decisive, and available when an adversary can suppress evidence. The monitor must therefore be able to abstain. We then distinguish two sources of incomplete evidence. Sequence numbers and periodic reports can identify missing events, whereas detecting silent streams requires timing assumptions. We also examine how membership changes and coordinator failures affect verdict soundness and recovery. We implement these mechanisms in a three-tier monitoring architecture using MQTT and NATS JetStream. Experiments with an LLM-planned robot swarm demonstrate the failure modes, show how the proposed mechanisms prevent unsupported compliance verdicts, and measure their runtime and communication costs.
item.dc:creator: Nikolaos Kekatos, Antonio Anastasio Bruto da Costa, Alexios Lekidis, Pabitra Mitra, Hosein Nazarpour, Priyanka Sinha

item.title: "I Do Intend to Deliver": Will LLMs Run a Marketplace Advance-Fee Scam?
item.description: arXiv:2611.32957v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Online fraud is traditionally limited by the cost of the human labor needed to talk to potential victims. We ask whether hosted large language models will now supply that labor. We prompted ten off-the-shelf models to play the seller in the "free item, just pay delivery" advance-fee scam common on buy-and-sell sites, using a plain system prompt with no jailbreak. Each model played 30 conversations against each of four buyer personas, from credulous to guarded, with the same model playing the buyer (1,200 conversations). We label each conversation by what happened to the buyer's money, and validate the labels against two human coders. 737 conversations (61%) ended with the buyer paying in advance. Eight of the ten models played in almost every conversation, and running both sides cost about 2.5 cents per payment. Only the guarded buyer, who wanted a findable identity, resisted, and the most willing sellers got past it by inventing names and phone numbers. Sellers that recognized the scam still took the money in 133 conversations, usually reasoning about their own honesty rather than the buyer's risk. Several models protected the buyer without refusing, by conceding payment on delivery, so refusal rates alone misstate safety. We release the benchmark, prompts, code and labels.
item.dc:creator: Megan Squire

item.title: SALSA: Sampling Adversarial Suffixes from Learned Distributions for LLM Safety Assessment
item.description: arXiv:2611.33030v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where adversaries append optimized suffixes to otherwise benign looking prompts to bypass safety alignment. Existing optimization-based GCG-style attacks can be effective, but they are expensive at inference time, and suffer from poor transfer. We present, SALSA, a generative framework that learns a distribution over jailbreak suffixes from optimization-derived attack corpora. Once trained, the model supports efficient sampling-based attacks. On open-source targets, it achieves attack success rates comparable to state-of-the-art optimization baselines, while reducing generation time from 3.46s to 0.04s per prompt. In black-box transfer, it remains highly effective against proprietary systems, including 99% ASR on GPT-3.5-Turbo, and reaches 45% ASR on the substantially harder GPT-4o, more than doubling the strongest baseline at an equal sampling budget. We further offer an intuition for why generative sampling can preserve high attack success, when the learned suffix distribution is close to the distribution of optimization outputs. Overall, our results show that learning adversarial suffix distributions yields a scalable, and practically efficient foundation for continuous LLM vulnerability discovery.
item.dc:creator: Shivank Rajput, Himanshu Singh, A. V. Subramanyam

item.title: VideoMark: Training-Free Watermarking for 2D-VAE Video Diffusion Models
item.description: arXiv:2504.16359v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work presents \textbf{VideoMark}, a training-free watermarking framework for video diffusion models with frame-aligned 2D VAEs. VideoMark embeds pseudorandom error-correcting (PRC) codewords by modulating the signs of Gaussian initialization noise without model retraining. Under a joint pseudorandomness assumption on the instantiated PRC encoder, the resulting initialization tensor is computationally indistinguishable from the Gaussian reference; exact distributional equality holds for the ideal independent uniform-sign construction. To support temporally structured video watermarking, we introduce a frame-wise message design together with a Temporal Matching Module (TMM), which recovers frame correspondence under temporal reordering without requiring length-specific watermark layouts. Experiments on ModelScope and I2VGen-XL show that VideoMark achieves accurate watermark extraction on clean generations while maintaining video quality comparable to watermark-free generation. The proposed temporal matching mechanism further improves recovery under frame reordering and enables systematic evaluation under a range of temporal and compression perturbations. We additionally analyze the computational characteristics and practical operating conditions of inversion-based extraction. Overall, VideoMark provides a simple training-free construction for studying pseudorandom watermarking in videos generated by frame-aligned 2D-VAE diffusion models, and establishes a foundation for extending structured noise watermarking to broader video-generation architectures.
item.dc:creator: Hanqian Li, Aiwei Liu, Jungang Li, Yu Huang, Chen Ling, Ye Pan, Shuliang Liu, Zheng Qi, Junhao Chen, Xuming Hu

item.title: PILOT: Command-line Interface Fuzzing via Path-Guided, Iterative Large Language Model Prompting
item.description: arXiv:2511.20555v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Command-line interface (CLI) fuzzing tests programs by mutating both command-line options and input file contents, thus enabling discovery of vulnerabilities that only manifest under specific option-input combinations. Prior works of CLI fuzzing face the challenges of generating semantics-rich option strings and input files, which cannot reach deeply embedded target functions. This often leads to a missed detection of such a deep vulnerability using existing CLI fuzzing techniques. In this paper, we design a novel Path-guided, Iterative LLM-Orchestrated Testing framework, called PILOT, to generate effective initial seeds for fuzzing CLI applications. The key insight is to provide potential call paths to target functions as context to LLM so that it can better generate CLI option strings and input files. Then, PILOT iteratively repeats the process, and provides reached functions as additional context so that target functions are reached. Our evaluation on real-world CLI applications demonstrates that PILOT, combined with existing fuzzers, achieves higher coverage than state-of-the-art fuzzing approaches and discovers 51 zero-day vulnerabilities. We responsibly disclosed all the vulnerabilities to their developers and so far 41 have been confirmed by their developers with 33 being fixed and five assigned CVE identifiers.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 2026 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP), San Francisco, CA, USA, 2026, pp. 3757-3775
item.dc:creator: Momoko Shiraishi, Yinzhi Cao, Takahiro Shinagawa

item.title: Granite: Granular Runtime Enforcement for GitHub Actions Permissions
item.description: arXiv:2512.11602v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: GitHub Actions is a popular CI/CD platform that lets maintainers build workflows from reusable third-party actions, organized into jobs of sequential steps. To control access to repository resources, GitHub enforces token permissions only at the job level. This violates the principle of least privilege: every step shares the job's full permissions, so a single compromised action can misuse all of them, as witnessed by the recent tj-actions compromise, enabling broader software supply chain attacks. We present Granite, the first system to enforce fine-grained, step-level permissions for GitHub Actions at runtime. Untrusted steps never hold the real token; a separate controller issues each step an identifier token and supplies the real token only to requests that meet the step's policy. Granite builds on GitHub's self-hosted runner, requires no workflow changes, and transparently handles JavaScript, composite, and Docker actions. Across 500 workflows (12,915 jobs) from the most-starred GitHub repositories, 46.3% of jobs are overprivileged and can be protected by Granite. On 46 repositories and 127 unique actions, Granite preserves the behavior of every job that runs on the unmodified runner, except one it blocks by design. Reproducing 10 permission-misuse attacks over 42 overprivileged jobs, including attempts to bypass its enforcement, Granite prevents all of them and removes write access from about 83.3% of the steps that hold it under GitHub's current model. Its average per-step overhead is 7.9%, making Granite a practical and effective tool to reduce the attack surface in CI/CD pipelines.
item.dc:creator: Mojtaba Moazen, Amir M. Ahmadian, Musard Balliu

item.title: VENOMREC: Cross-Modal Interactive Poisoning for Targeted Promotion in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems
item.description: arXiv:2602.06409v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are pushing recommender systems (RecSys) toward content-grounded retrieval and ranking via cross-modal fusion. We find that while cross-modal consensus often mitigates conventional poisoning that manipulates interaction logs or perturbs a single modality, it also introduces a new attack surface where synchronised multimodal poisoning can reliably steer fused representations along stable semantic directions during fine-tuning. To characterise this threat, we formalise cross-modal interactive poisoning and propose VENOMREC, which performs Exposure Alignment to identify high-exposure regions in the joint embedding space and Cross-modal Interactive Perturbation to craft attention-guided coupled token--patch edits. Experiments on four real-world multimodal datasets demonstrate that VENOMREC consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving 0.73 mean ER@20 and improving over the strongest baseline by +0.52 absolute ER points on average, while maintaining comparable recommendation utility. Code is available at https://github.com/GuoweiGuan666/VenomRec.
item.dc:creator: Guowei Guan, Yurong Hao, Jiaming Zhang, Tiantong Wu, Fuyao Zhang, Tianxiang Chen, Longtao Huang, Cyril Leung, Wei Yang Bryan Lim

item.title: Beyond True or False: Why You Can't Trust the Reasoning in LLM-Generated Vulnerability Reports
item.description: arXiv:2602.06687v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When a state-of-the-art LLM labels a function as vulnerable, can we trust its explanation? This paper first reveals a worrisome fact: 30.3% of correct verdicts from LLMs are produced through \textit{hallucinated or causally wrong reasoning}. While prior work has partially observed this phenomenon, no study has quantified its prevalence, taxonomized its failure modes, or proposed a structural fix. We aim to address all three. First, we construct reasoning-level datasets: real-world vulnerabilities across 149 CWE types annotated with evidence-based reasoning chains, and semantically equivalent code perturbations for robustness testing. Through open coding of 400 reasoning traces across 10 LLMs, we identify 12 systematic failure modes, among which code comprehension and logical reasoning errors are the most prevalent. Motivated by these findings, we propose DagVul, which models vulnerability reasoning as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) generation task, enforcing causal dependencies between reasoning steps and aligning them with program semantics via Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). DagVul improves reasoning F1-score by an average of 13.3% over baselines. Our 8B-parameter model achieves performance comparable to Claude-Sonnet-4.5 under CWE-Guided prompting (78.90% vs. 76.11%) in the evaluated setting. These results support the combined benefits of structured causal reasoning and training on curated, task-specific data for vulnerability analysis.
item.dc:creator: Li Lu, Yanjie Zhao, Hongzhou Rao, Kechi Zhang, Zhou Yang, Haoyu Wang

item.title: MASCing: Configurable Mixture-of-Experts Behavior via Activation Steering Masks
item.description: arXiv:2604.27818v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) operate under safety requirements that vary across applications and evolve with emerging threats and deployment policies. Conventional training-based interventions make adapting model behavior computationally expensive. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models introduce a further control challenge because each input activates only a subset of experts, coupling safety behavior to discrete routing decisions. Rapid adaption of MoE LLMs therefore requires a lightweight mechanism for identifying and controlling the routing decisions that produce the target behavior. We present MASCing (MoE Activation Steering Configuration), a framework that enables flexible configuration of safety-related MoE behavior without training the underlying model. MASCing uses an LSTM surrogate model to capture cross-layer dependencies and map routing logits to downstream behaviors. Guided by this surrogate, it identifies safety-relevant experts and optimizes a sparse steering mask to bias expert selection. This enables targeted enhancement or suppression of specific behaviors while preserving model utility. We evaluate MASCing on three contrasting safety objectives and observe consistent gains across seven MoE models. For multi-turn jailbreak defense, it improves the average defense success rate from 52.5% to 83.9%. For adult-content generation, MASCing enables models to comply with such requests that would otherwise be refused, increasing the average generation success rate from 52.6% to 82.0%. For political neutrality, MASCing makes models decline to state personal opinions on political questions, which they otherwise often give, raising the share of such questions on which they take no position from 31.8% to 75.4% while other questions remain answered. These results establish MASCing as a practical, lightweight, and flexible framework for task-specific safety configuration in MoE models.
item.dc:creator: Jona te Lintelo, Lichao Wu, Marina Kr\v{c}ek, Sengim Karayal\c{c}in, Stjepan Picek

item.title: The Best-Laid SCHEMEs: Coordinated Sabotage and Monitoring in Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2605.29178v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As agentic coding systems decompose work across multiple model instances, a critical safety question is whether those instances can coordinate to achieve a hidden malicious objective while appearing aligned with user intent. We introduce SCHEME, a benchmark of 11 task pairings across 7 settings built on real open-source libraries, each connecting a legitimate software-engineering task with a malicious side task. Side tasks are designed so that no proper subset of agents can complete them alone: agents must decompose a shared plan, relay partial requirements, and make mutually consistent edits. Evaluating ten frontier models, we find that coordinated sabotage is already practical, with models completing the malicious objective while succeeding on the legitimate task in 49\% to 85\% of trajectories. Stronger models also run into fewer communication failures and recover from more of them. However, trusted monitors that see the agents' code and communication catch at least 93\% of successful sabotage from every model, and telling the agents about the monitor lowers their sabotage success while barely helping them evade these monitors. Successful evasion requires an attacker optimized against the monitor. An automated red-teaming attacker hides 63\% of the sabotage that GPT 5.1 Codex Mini catches, but this transfers poorly to Claude Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 3 Flash monitors.
item.dc:creator: Nikolay Radev, Lennart Haas, Benjamin Arnav, Pablo Bernabeu-P\'erez

item.title: Selection Integrity for LLM Graph Memory: An Accumulability Criterion for Information-Flow-Blind Retrieval
item.description: arXiv:2606.12290v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agent memory is moving to graphs, and the provenance defenses now being built for it all check one thing: the provenance of the records an agent retrieves. We show that this entire class of defense is blind by construction. A long-term graph memory runs a global selection step over writable graph structure, so structure that an untrusted principal writes changes \emph{which} authenticated facts are selected while the cited evidence stays fully authenticated; faithful information-flow control (IFC), checking the provenance of what the reader uses (all of it authenticated), makes the byte-identical decision to no defense at all, across document-QA substrates and real multi-session agent memory. In the most consequential instance, a no-source structural write silently misdirects $28$ irreversible ledger transfers over $499$ live actions: faithful IFC permits every one, and \authselect\ prevents every one. We then characterize exactly which memories are exposed: a selector admits the channel when its structural term can reallocate an $\Omega(1)$ share of top-$k$ membership past a selected fact's margin. Personalized PageRank can, since a sourceless write reroutes conserved random-walk mass; a content-fixed reranker cannot, and Graphiti's node-distance, which leans on structure \emph{more} than PageRank does, stays immune. Reallocatability, not reliance, is the predictor. We prove the immune case in general and the open case under a chokepoint condition we verify. Closing the channel forces any provenance defense to recompute selection on the authenticated subgraph, which is what \authselect\ does, at zero over-block and $2$--$3\%$ latency.
item.dc:creator: Zeming Fei, Hongming Fei, Xiaoyang Wang, Yang yang, Prosanta Gope, Biplab Sikdar, Ying Zhang

item.title: Merging Cyber Threat Intelligence Through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Small Language Models for Rich Threat Representation
item.description: arXiv:2609.07280v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cybersecurity operations rely on CTI from heterogeneous sources, such as structured threat representations and narrative reports. They describe adversarial behaviors but rarely make explicit the conditions that enable each attack step, the consequences it produces, and the evidence supporting them, leaving analysts to correlate fragmented information manually. Existing approaches extract entities, map tactics and techniques, or reconstruct attack chains; enriching attack steps with explicit, evidence-linked semantics remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a local-first pipeline for evidence-grounded attack-step enrichment that combines hybrid RAG with a locally deployed SLM. Starting from an analyst-provided attack representation and supporting CTI documents, the pipeline retrieves step-relevant evidence and generates enriched descriptions, pre-conditions, post-conditions, and traceable links to the supporting passages. The enriched steps are organized into graph that groups MITRE ATT&CK-aligned steps into tactic-level milestones. Explicit conditions help defenders block attacks by removing their enabling conditions and support detection by checking for their expected consequences. We evaluate the pipeline on ten public malware case studies derived from UK NCSC reports, using automated measurements and a structured manual assessment with annotations from two annotators. The results demonstrate that the pipeline is effective at generating conditions that are, for the most part, evidence-supported and meaningful w.r.t. the analyzed attack step. Similar considerations hold for the enriched descriptions. Finally, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of locally generating structured, evidence-grounded enrichments that improve the interpretability and traceability of attack step representations without requiring a manual reconstruction of attack execution.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Deidda, Leonardo Regano, Alessandro Sanna, Davide Maiorca, Giorgio Giacinto

item.title: Principled Detection of Coordinated Manipulation from Aggregate Distortion and Account Reuse
item.description: arXiv:2609.13407v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coordinated manipulation is collective: plausible accounts can jointly distort ratings, rankings, and engagement. Existing defenses primarily construct evidence from identities, graphs, content, or co-activity. We introduce an aggregate-first evidence layer that treats distortion of a context-level outcome distribution as the primary evidence object. The engine observes only a histogram, count, resolution, and reference distribution; identities are withheld until interval evidence is fixed. Because raw discrepancies have positive finite-sample expectation, we subtract a matched null expectation to obtain signed evidence and account for reference uncertainty. Participation logs then accumulate these fixed increments across accounts. We characterize matched-exposure divergence, bound self-influence, establish finite-horizon separation, and derive an exact linear reuse law for paired contexts. We evaluate the mechanism with controlled rotation experiments and paired counterfactual interventions on historical Amazon review streams. Historical reviews provide the behavioral background; synthetic identities provide known coalition membership, and exact clean twins provide counterfactual controls. In a fixed-attack sweep against historical non-donor comparison accounts, reassigning the same manipulated events across identities with increasing reuse raises account-score ROC-AUC from 0.500 to 0.797. With activity- and exposure-matched clean twins, frequency is at chance while counterfactual attribution achieves ROC-AUC 0.744. Under a mean-preserving shape intervention, Wasserstein-1 and Jensen-Shannon evidence achieve ROC-AUC 0.909 and 0.967, while frequency and mean-based attribution remain at chance. Aggregate evidence complements repeated co-activity, improving mixed-mechanism ROC-AUC from 0.750 to 0.874 with a simple untrained combination.
item.dc:creator: Qian Guo, Yidan Hu, Rui Zhang

item.title: How Attackers Launder Funds through Mixers: Characterization and Detection on Ethereum
item.description: arXiv:2609.27807v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mixers protect privacy by concealing deposit--withdrawal links, but are also abused to launder illicit funds. Existing anti-money laundering studies do not specifically target mixer laundering, while mixer research focuses on deanonymization rather than identifying laundering-related transactions. Public reports remain fragmented, leaving no public case-level dataset for systematic measurement and detection. To fill this void, this paper presents the first comprehensive study of mixer laundering on Ethereum. We first construct \textsc{MixLaunder}, the first public case-level dataset of mixer laundering. It covers 27 cases involving Tornado Cash and Railgun from 2020 to 2025 and labels 9,300 laundering-related transactions with case identities and observable upstream and downstream fund flows, including deposits totaling approximately \$1.1 billion. By comparing these transactions with background mixer usage, we identify five common strategies, showing that laundering evidence spans complementary behavioral and fund-flow contexts, while same-case activity is locally tight but weakly connected across bursts. Our analysis further reveals coverage gaps in mixer-side risk screening and representative deanonymization heuristics. Guided by these findings, we develop \textsc{MixGuard}, which combines tri-view representation learning with two-stage grouping for transaction-level detection and case-aware grouping. Under strict case-level holdout evaluation, \textsc{MixGuard} outperforms representative baselines, achieving 97.89\% detection precision and 98.73\% group purity, while its top ten groups cover 95.09\% of each case's transactions on average.
item.dc:creator: Qishuang Fu, Hang Zheng, Xihan Xiong, Joseph K. Liu, Yixin Liu, Shirui Pan, Qin Wang, Weiqing Wang, Zhipeng Wang, Tsz Hon Yuen

item.title: Made to Measure: Designing Image Watermarks to Specification
item.description: arXiv:2610.00780v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Image watermarking enables provenance and attribution, but practical deployments must jointly satisfy robustness, false-positive rate (FPR), image quality, and latency requirements. Existing watermarking methods offer complementary robustness against different attacks, making their composition attractive for broader protection. However, combining watermarks introduces interference, distortion, decoding overhead, and additional verification paths that share the same FPR budget. We propose TAILOR, a request-conditioned watermark composition framework with three stages: (1) offline characterization models fragment recovery, distortion, latency, and composition interactions across embedding strengths; (2) joint configuration selection uses satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) to jointly optimize fragment selection, continuous embedding strengths, embedding order, and geometric recovery while minimizing predicted distortion; and (3) live calibration validates candidate configurations on user images and refines inaccurate offline predictions to improve deployment success. Across 7,321 distinct deployment requests spanning five scenarios and 20 attack settings, TAILOR achieves 96.21% scenario-averaged request satisfaction with a mean PSNR of 41.02 dB, demonstrating its effectiveness in meeting diverse deployment requirements while maintaining high image fidelity. Code is available at https://github.com/aaFrostnova/Tailor.
item.dc:creator: Mingzhe Li, Yuefeng Peng, Kejing Xia, Pranav Jeyakumar, Ruolan Leslie Famularo, Shiqing Ma

item.title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks
item.description: arXiv:2610.24052v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 3.4% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 82.4% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly under both their feedback monitor and GPT-5.6 Sol in at most 32% of executions, compared with 82% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.
item.dc:creator: John Kitaoka, Thao Amelia Pham, Carlos Rafael Giudice, Jacob Merizian

item.title: The Missing Compliance Class: LLM Graders That Collapse Jailbreak Success, and a Free Check
item.description: arXiv:2610.24872v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Jailbreak evaluations often substitute open-weight 7B to 9B instruction-tuned models as local, deterministic judges for frontier APIs. Holding target models, prompts, responses, and a four-class rubric fixed across eight graders from five organizations, we find that dense 8B and 9B judges collapse compliant responses onto evasion. One assigns compliance zero times in 900 responses while agreeing with our reference judge on 78.0% of items, certifying an unsafe model as safe. This collapse holds across four 900-response corpora, multiplying reported compliance by a factor of 22 to 25 on our primary corpora while non-refusal shifts by 18.0 to 23.0 points. Without the three collapsing graders, compliance varies by 1.7x to 2.8x across all four corpora, whereas post-labelling rubric rulings (+16.3 points) and benchmark choice (15.3 points) still shift non-refusal. Per-class label counts expose class collapse at zero cost without human labels, motivating an eight-item reporting minimum that pairs compliance with non-refusal rates.
item.dc:creator: Ruqiya Bin Safi

item.title: Deletion Is Not Substitution: Component Attribution in a Layered Prompt-Injection Gateway for LLM Tool Calls
item.description: arXiv:2610.33198v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Prompt-injection defenses for LLM agents are commonly built as cascades of increasingly costly stages, and ablation studies evaluate their components by switching each stage off and counting the detections lost. In a cascade, however, stages are not independent: a stage's contribution depends on what is routed to it and how its verdicts are enforced, so deletion-based ablation can mislead. We test this on BARBICAN, a four-tier, fail-closed gateway for Model Context Protocol tool calls, developed in our group, that routes borderline inputs to a neural arbitrator. After reproducing its recorded evaluation exactly, we apply deletion, constant substitution, repair and transplant to its arbitration stage. The findings rest on over thirty instrumented runs over 25,000 prompts, two platforms, an independent check set and six versions from the system's history. Depending on how "switching off" is defined, deletion credits the stage with contributions that differ by more than an order of magnitude, whereas substitution shows that its verdicts can affect only a few inputs, all attacks. Neither repairing the stage nor replacing it with a much stronger classifier changed the system appreciably: its influence is set by its position, not its quality. An observation that bounds the decisions a routed stage can change explains this, and a cascade of public classifiers reproduces it whenever routing concentrates attacks. Treating constant verdicts as mutants, we derive a continuous-integration gate that detects a stage whose verdicts cannot reach the output and, in light of these results, offer a three-point roadmap for ablation studies.
item.dc:creator: \.Ipek Abas{\i}kele\c{s} Turgut, Edip G\"um\"u\c{s}

item.title: O2N2: Efficient Doubly Oblivious Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
item.description: arXiv:2611.03415v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Privacy-preserving approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search allows clients to search from an untrusted server without revealing sensitive queries, and is useful in scenarios like medical diagnostics and credit scoring. Among the various privacy-preserving primitives, trusted execution environments (TEEs) have much lower overhead than heavy cryptographic ones, yet they leak memory access patterns, enabling adversaries to infer query contents. Oblivious RAM (ORAM) can be used to hide those access patterns at $\mathrm{O}(\log N)$ asymptotic cost, but existing high-performance ANN search algorithms (e.g., IVF or HNSW) exhibit complex, data-dependent access patterns that are unfriendly for ORAM. Furthermore, standard ORAM constructions typically assume there exists a small amount of trusted storage, which weakens the security guarantees and is not always feasible. Solutions that eliminate such trusted storage (known as {\em double obliviousness}) typically degrade performance further to $\mathrm{O}(\log^2 N)$. We introduce O2N2, a doubly oblivious ANN framework built around single-path search in randomly rotated $k$-d tree forests. A pointer-based Circuit ORAM stores the search structure, with separate storage for compact internal nodes and vector-bearing leaves. Each visited leaf is processed by an oblivious selection network, and fixed-schedule duplicate removal and selection combine the local results into the final top-$k$. We evaluate O2N2 on real-world datasets and further test its scalability on 100 million vectors. For 10-NN and 100-NN search at the specified high-recall targets, it achieves a $9.8$--$125.9\times$ speedup over the fastest doubly oblivious baselines. It also achieves comparable efficiency against existing singly oblivious systems such as Compass (OSDI~'25) and BiSON (EuroS\&P~'26), while providing stronger privacy guarantees.
item.dc:creator: Zhechen Li, Zimai Guo, Mingxun Zhou, Chang Shi, Cheng Hong

item.title: QUASI: Post-Quantum Quorum Attestation of Pre-Validated Statements
item.description: arXiv:2611.10403v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present QUASI, a newly conceived class of hash-based, post-quantum-secure protocols that enable a group of parties to produce a publicly verifiable attestation about a pre-validated statement. QUASI produces attestations that reduce the size and verification cost to a fraction of a full hash-based signatures collection, without relying on SNARKs or a trusted setup. QUASI rests on a surprising discovery: each party need not sign the entire statement. Authenticating only a small subset of symbols suffices for a quorum to attest to the whole. We turn this insight into a randomized construction that achieves reductions of more than 10x in per-party contribution size and hash computations for generation and verification, compared with full hash-based signatures. QUASI is a generic primitive supporting diverse applications. Operationally, QUASI requires no additional interactive setup or preprocessing beyond independent key generation by parties for the underlying hash-based authentication scheme. Two principal use cases are external attestation for signature-free consensus, enabling clients to verify statements about committed state; and preprocessing for SNARK-based aggregation, compounding QUASI's savings with succinct-proof compression.
item.dc:creator: Maksym Ioffe, Dahlia Malkhi

item.title: From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses
item.description: arXiv:2611.13960v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets so that agents can resolve issues and run tests. That coupling turns the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary can inject instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload rather than a vulnerability to be separately exploited. We argue that security in agentic systems is not an emergent behavioral property of individual language models, but a structural property of the cognitive architecture and of the composition of permissions across interacting agents and humans. Static regex blacklists miss flag permutations and structural attacks, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails ask a second model to guess physical invariants at tens to hundreds of milliseconds per call while over-blocking benign work. We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture organized around Separation of Intelligence and Authority across four pillars: (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings; (2) a product taint lattice L_trust x L_sens and a compositional Separation-of-Duties ledger over shared workspace provenance; (3) deterministic OS/subprocess guards; and (4) extended bytecode certificates, split-horizon dual-key audit logs, a self-healing verification loop (CodeVerifier, DualModelReviewer, SecurityTestSynthesizer), and a progressive pedagogical UserWikiManager. On N=252 fixtures and a 12+12 multi-step trajectory suite, Ring 0 achieves FPR=0.000 (0.939 unfitted out-of-sample / 0.962 OS-inert; 1.000 post-audit conformance ABR) in 31.5 us median latency (4,517x faster than a live local LLM-judge) and blocks 12/12 multi-step kill chains at 0.000 benign trajectory FPR (266.7 us/step; ~24 us/step O(1) ledger state folding).
item.dc:creator: Simon Hegelich, Habiba Sarhan, Morteza Shahrezaye, Kolja Hegelich, Christian Montag, Ralf Schneider, Erik Cambria

item.title: Asymmetric Optical Image Watermarking
item.description: arXiv:2611.23350v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Watermark detectors held by a provider cannot be checked by third parties, and a party that can detect a mark can usually also forge it. We study a two-layer image watermark in which the Fourier transform at the core of the pipeline is performed by a coherent optical 4F unit. Layer 1 carries an Ed25519 signature bound to the image content in Fourier magnitudes, so anyone with the public key verifies offline. Layer 2 is a key-defined carrier written by a secret phase hologram and read by a matched-filter correlator. The optics is a scalar-diffraction simulation with finite modulator bits, pixel aperture, pupil, defocus, misalignment, and sensor noise. No hardware is built. All criteria were fixed in a hashed specification before any optical result. The simulated optical signer reproduces the digital pipeline (field error 1.7e-15, bit agreement 99.997%), verifies at least 99.5% of 877 images under each of 8 post-sensor settings, one unattacked, and accepts none of 40,670 unmarked images. The optical carrier is key-selective: the matched key detects it on 99.8% of the unattacked images, and detection falls to 0% under a scale error of 1% and to 0% under a mask shift of 1 bin. Security rests on the signature and the content binding, for which we separate what is provable from what is measured.
item.dc:creator: Guang Yang

item.title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
item.description: arXiv:2611.25509v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

item.title: Visual Attribution Limits and Graded Provenance Auditing in Commercial Video-Generation APIs
item.description: arXiv:2611.26508v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Commercial video-generation APIs bill by model and tier, while intermediaries could substitute cheaper models, lower tiers, or cached clips. What can a delivered file establish about its origin? We combine measurements of passive attribution and cryptographic provenance into a graded audit. We test attribution probes and zero-shot detectors under re-encoding, downscaling, and frame-rate changes, and survey C2PA and GB 45438 metadata across 19 commercial endpoints. Only authenticated provenance supports accusations: tier contradictions or duplicate signed instances under fresh-generation contracts, excluding retries and idempotent returns. Unverifiable signed-endpoint deliveries trigger original-file demands under pass-through clauses; archive-reuse and delivery-parameter screens support review only. Six-model container and bitstream accuracy falls from 83.9% on raw files to 45.3% after uniform re-encoding, using different feature sets. Subsampling real references from 24 to 3 fps raises pooled D3 AUROC from 0.845 to 0.988. Only BytePlus authenticates tier claims under our pinned policy, including 187/187 audited deliveries across three Seedance tiers; tested remuxing and re-encoding leave processed Seedance files unverifiable. The audit identifies authenticated contradictions in 100/100 raw 720p signed tier-swap cases, with zero observed false flags on the tested honest pools.
item.dc:creator: Haocheng Mei, Yuchuan Tian, Yingte Shu, Chao Xu, Kai Han, Allen Chen, Yunhe Wang

item.title: Reporting Differential Privacy Guarantees via Operationally Equivalent $\varepsilon$: What Does $\varepsilon=19.61$ Mean for the 2020 U.S. Census?
item.description: arXiv:2611.28790v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The large value $\varepsilon=19.61$, reported as an approximate differential privacy (ADP) parameter for the 2020 U.S. Census, has prompted doubts about the adequacy of Census privacy protection. This value was obtained by converting component guarantees expressed in zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), an extension of differential privacy (DP), to ADP at $\delta=10^{-10}$. Summarizing a guarantee by a single $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ pair can substantially loosen its upper bound on the power (true positive rate) of a distinguishing test at a given significance level. We express the power bound from the original guarantee as the $\alpha$-operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$, the smallest pure DP parameter yielding the same power bound at significance level $\alpha$. The full operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$ curve represents the original bound exactly on $(0,1)$, even when that bound is nonconcave. We also characterize the curve's extrema over an interval of significance levels. When finite, they give the pure DP parameters whose power bounds enclose the original bound on that interval. The mapping preserves the ordering of guarantees by their power bounds at each significance level, whereas conversion to single ADP pairs or Gaussian DP (GDP) envelopes can reverse this ordering for Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms with equal noise variance. For the P.L. 94-171 redistricting data, we reproduce the reported $\varepsilon=19.61$ as the sum of rounded component ADP values. The published zCDP guarantee yields operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$ values of approximately $4.25$, $2.94$, and $3.18$ at significance levels of $1\%$, $5\%$, and $10\%$, respectively. These values convey the original guarantee's constraints on distinguishing attacks more clearly than does the reported value $\varepsilon=19.61$, which by itself places little restriction on the success of such attacks.

item.title: DuetFHE: Compiling Dual-Lane Nonlinear Circuits for Complex-Packed CKKS Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.29350v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Complex packing in CKKS stores two real streams in the real and imaginary lanes of each slot. Direct squaring couples the lanes, while squaring them separately requires two ciphertext-ciphertext multiplications (HMults). DuetFHE is a GPU compiler that uses a phase transformation to square both lanes independently with one HMult. It reuses dual-lane squares in polynomial activations and the modular-reduction stage of CKKS bootstrapping. The compiler further plans ciphertext scales and reuses conjugates to sustain the complex-packed representation across stages. On a single RTX 5090, DuetFHE accelerates four polynomial activations by $1.60$--$1.79\times$ over direct evaluation on two real ciphertexts. For two-image AESPA ResNet-20 inference, it maintains packed execution across convolutions, square activations, and bootstrapping, achieving a $1.97\times$ end-to-end speedup over the fastest tested EasyFHE batched baseline on both the RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000.
item.dc:creator: Ke Chang, Jian Wang, Xuan Xu, Jiqiang Liu

item.title: NPUFHE: An Efficient CKKS Execution System for Ascend NPUs
item.description: arXiv:2611.29353v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables computation directly on encrypted data, but its substantial computational cost hinders adoption in privacy-preserving artificial intelligence (AI) applications. Neural processing units (NPUs) already deployed in AI infrastructure provide a practical platform for FHE acceleration. However, after mapping the number theoretic transform (NTT) to matrix multiplications on Ascend NPUs, modular arithmetic and representation conversion on the Vector backend still incur substantial overhead at stage boundaries. Evaluation-key material of key switching also increases storage and data-transfer costs, and whole-limb task assignment causes tail load imbalance. We present NPUFHE, an end-to-end CKKS execution system optimized for Ascend NPUs. To reduce modular recovery and twiddle costs in NTT, we propose Boundary-Optimized NTT, which eliminates intra-axis modular recovery, compiles intra-axis twiddle factors into matrix constants, and introduces two-level folded modular recovery at axis endpoints. To alleviate evaluation-key storage and transfer pressure, we design Compact Shoup encoding, which halves the key representation through local coefficient recovery. Finally, we propose Cost-Aware Parallel Tiling to mitigate tail load imbalance caused by whole-limb task assignment. It uses a cost model to adaptively partition tail tasks and smooth stepwise latency increases. We integrate the above designs into OpenFHE. On one Ascend 910B4, full-packing CKKS bootstrapping with real evaluation keys takes 0.95 s, encrypted CIFAR-10 ResNet-20 inference with bootstrapping requires 9.87 s per image, and encrypted MNIST inference achieves an amortized latency of 19.81 ms per image. The peak NTT throughput of NPUFHE reaches up to $184.22\times$, $2.04\times$, and $4.46\times$ that of OpenFHE on CPU, TensorFHE, and CROSS, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Ke Chang, Jian Wang, Xuan Xu, Yijing Zong, Jiqiang Liu

item.title: Packing Stern into L2: GPU-Accelerated Primal-Shortened ISD for High-Codimension Binary Goppa Key Recovery
item.description: arXiv:2611.29958v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Primal-Shortened Information-Set Decoding (ISD) with quadratic polar lifting recently pushed TII McEliece Track-2 key recovery to $mt=126$ (TII-228, $2{,}463$ CPU core-hours), with over $99\%$ of runtime spent harvesting weight-$(2t+1)$ codewords. Porting MiniMax's Mode-6 Stern sampler directly to one block per SM leaves $1.0\text{-}1.5\text{ GB}$ of hash tables active and stalls on global memory. We pack $128$ syndrome bits into one $16$-byte ulonglong2 without left-triple indices (lossless for $mt \le 145$, and extended to $mt \le 192$ via truncated range pre-filtering), share $G \in \{4, 8\}$ cooperative tables inside GPU L2 cache, batch $64G$ random systematic reductions per launch, and widen the shortening prefix $n'$ to cut modeled GPU-hours by $34\%\text{-}47\%$. Across five Track-2 challenges ($mt = 108 \to 153$), every recovered private key passes both the official SageMath checker and a standalone pure-Python verifier. Eight Modal L40S GPUs solve TII-228 ($mt=126$) in $18.9\text{ min}$ ($2.15$ GPU-hours, $3.0\times$ faster in wall-clock than MiniMax's EPYC cluster). We further recover keys for the previously undocumented challenges TII-237 ($mt=135$, $22.1$ L4 GPU-hours), TII-235 ($mt=144$, $39.62$ L40S GPU-hours, $17.97\text{ s}$ lift), and TII-185 ($mt=153$, $140.4$ L40S + $\approx 60$ L4 GPU-hours, $39.01\text{ s}$ lift). These results do not demonstrate practical recovery against Classic McEliece parameters ($mt \ge 768$).
