item.title: Fail-Closed Alignment for Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2602.16977v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We identify a structural weakness in current large language model (LLM) alignment: refusal mechanisms in these models are fail-open. While existing approaches tend to encode refusal behaviors across multiple latent features, suppressing a single feature (via prompt-based jailbreaks) is sufficient to collapse alignment, leading to unsafe generation. Motivated by this, we propose fail-closed alignment as a design principle for robust LLM safety: refusal mechanisms should remain effective even under partial failures via redundant, independent causal pathways. We present a concrete instantiation of this principle: a progressive alignment framework that iteratively identifies and ablates previously learned refusal directions, forcing the model to reconstruct safety along new, independent subspaces. Across six jailbreak attacks, our method achieves the lowest observed average attack success rate (1.6%) while largely preserving generation quality and preventing excessive over-refusals, with negligible computational overhead. Additional analyses confirm that models trained with our method encode multiple, causally independent refusal directions that prompt-based jailbreaks cannot fully suppress, providing empirical support for fail-closed alignment as a principled foundation for robust LLM safety. Our code for reproducing the results is available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-and-Responsible-AI-Lab/Fail-Closed-Alignment

item.title: Differential Privacy for Network Connectedness Indices
item.description: arXiv:2603.15609v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Researchers increasingly use data on social and economic networks to study a range of social science questions, but releasing statistics derived from networks can raise significant privacy concerns. We show how to release network connectedness indices that quantify assortative mixing across node attributes under edge-adjacent differential privacy. Directly adding noise to connectedness indices based on global sensitivity can result in poor accuracy both because connectedness indices have high global sensitivity and because a single node's attribute can potentially be an input to connectedness in thousands of cells, leading to poor composition. Our method, which is straightforward to apply, first randomizes node attributes, then analytically debiases downstream statistics, and finally adds noise to protect the presence or absence of individual edges. We prove consistency and asymptotic normality of our estimators for both discrete and continuous labels and show our method works well in simulations and on real networks with as few as 200 nodes collected by social scientists.
item.dc:creator: Tom A. Rutter, Yuxin Liu, M. Amin Rahimian

item.title: FLIPS: Instance-Fingerprinting for LLMs via Pseudo-random Sequences
item.description: arXiv:2606.03330v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Literature reveals that a Large Language Model's (LLM) behavior is not only conditioned by its original weights but also its instance-level parameters, such as instructional prompt, sampling configuration or quantization. A model that generates safe outputs under one configuration may produce toxic content under another. However, current LLM identification techniques (such as fingerprinting) focus on intellectual property protection, and their design favors robustness to changes in these instance-level parameters. This poses a critical challenge for AI regulation in which compliance assessments target actual deployed behaviors, not model provenance. In this paper, we introduce instance-level fingerprinting, a regulator-oriented paradigm that distinguishes configurations of the same LLM. Our method, FLIPS, exploits biases in generated binary random sequences. On a benchmark of 237 model instances, it identifies the instance with 77% accuracy from 32 queries to the target, against at most 33% for the adapted LLMmap baseline. Recognizing that a target is unseen, also called open-set challenge, is much harder. When 10% of instances are unseen, FLIPS realises a recall of 41% on the unseen instances, at a precision of 23%, i.e. more than twice better than random. Closed-set instance fingerprinting is thus practical with a few dozen queries, whereas the open-set setting remains an open problem. Code available at https://github.com/GurvanR/FLIPS-LLM-Instance-Fingerprinting.

item.title: From Reconnaissance to Response: Quantitative Risk Parameterization and Game Theoretic Containment in Modern Enterprise Attack
item.description: arXiv:2609.36485v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern Security Operations Centers struggle with delayed manual incident response, enabling adversaries to advance through the Cyber Kill Chain during early stage reconnaissance. While classical game theoretic defense models optimize strategic resource allocation, they rely on static utility matrices that fail to adapt to dynamic telemetry. This paper presents an integrated, metrics driven decision engine that bridges quantitative risk parameterization and continuous automated response time. Common Vulnerability Scoring Systems exploitability parameters are mapped to attacker success probabilities and evaluate defender log distributions via Factor Analysis of Information Risk Monte Carlo simulations. Real time SIEM logs streams are modeled as Poisson process arrival rates, dynamically updating defender posterior threat belief through sequential Bayesian filtering. A closed form threshold is derived by framing the interaction as a dynamic Bayesian Stackelberg game, where the expected unmitigated risk exceeds proactive containment cost. Parameterized against empirical data from the 2023 MGM Resorts and Caesars Entertainment cyber incident, simulation results demonstrate that the engine suppresses transient background noise while triggering automated SOAR network isolation within seconds of adversarial probing. Multi parameter sensitivity analysis confirms that the decision boundary dynamically adjusts to live perimeter vulnerability, offering a control theoretic foundation for sub minute automated threat containment.
item.dc:creator: Shadeeb Hossain, Elias Calboreanu

item.title: $\mathsf{EFI}\Leftrightarrow\mathsf{1PRS}$
item.description: arXiv:2610.18799v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A series of recent works has established EFI pairs as the "minimal" assumption for quantum cryptography. Recently, Cavalar et al. [CCC+26] showed that EFI pairs are equivalent to non-uniform expanding single-copy pseudorandom state generators (1PRS), and obtained a non-uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. We remove the non-uniformity in their construction and prove that EFI pairs are equivalent to expanding 1PRS. As a corollary, we obtain the first uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. Together with the equivalence of statistically verifiable one-way state generators and commitments proved by Batra and Jain [BJ24], this gives a quantum analogue of the classical equivalence between one-way functions, commitments, and pseudorandom generators.

item.title: DeepAVR: Deep Analysis via Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Vulnerability Repair
item.description: arXiv:2610.32345v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) has emerged as a promising approach to identifying and fixing software vulnerabilities autonomously. Early LLM-based approaches focused on patch generation under the assumption of perfect fault localization, while recent end-to-end methods attempt to repair vulnerabilities directly from sanitizer logs. However, these methods often fail when the root cause is deeply hidden, either physically distant from the crash site or logically masked by interdependent errors, making the initial report insufficient. We propose DeepAVR, a multi-agent framework that transforms intermediate repair outcomes into structured diagnostic feedback. It coordinates specialized agents for fault localization, patch generation, compilation, security and functionality validation, and patch review to iteratively refine localization and patch hypotheses. Specifically, DeepAVR introduces patch-conditioned re-localization, using execution results from intermediate patches to uncover hidden root causes, and root-cause-oriented patch review to identify symptom-level fixes and incomplete repairs that escape execution-based validation. Evaluation on VulnLoc, a real-world C/C++ vulnerability repair dataset, shows that DeepAVR outperforms prior methods, generating correct patches for 92.3% of vulnerabilities. Evaluation on SAN2VULN demonstrates its ability to repair vulnerabilities unseen during training. On SEC-bench, DeepAVR outperforms the evaluated baselines on cases whose fixes lie outside the crash-site function.
item.dc:creator: Woorim Han, Hyunjun Kim, Brian Junekyu Lee, Kyeongmin Kim, Younghan Lee, Hyungon Moon, Yunheung Paek

item.title: Demystifying Prompt Stealing Attacks against Synthetic Video
item.description: arXiv:2611.00102v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Creators publicly showcase generated content to advertise and sell their work, but these examples may also enable unauthorized reproduction and customization. We study whether an adversary can derive reusable inputs from a single public video for faithful reconstruction and controlled editing, without access to the original prompt or generator. We adapt captioning and prompt optimization approaches to video prompt stealing attacks (PSAs) and find that prompt recovery alone provides limited reconstruction fidelity. Even the original prompt produces different spatial and temporal realizations when the initial noise changes. Using an independent generator enlarges the reconstruction gap, as reusing the original prompt and seed can still produce substantially different videos. We propose V-PSA, which uses a recovered caption and DDIM inversion to construct a reference trajectory under an independent generator. Null-Text Inversion then optimizes per-step unconditional embeddings to reduce deviations from this trajectory during reconstruction. The resulting inputs also guide generation when the caption is modified, supporting edits that change selected content while preserving the target's layout and motion. We construct a benchmark containing 12,000 video-prompt pairs from three victim generators and four prompt sources. V-PSA achieves video-to-video similarity around 0.9 between target and reconstructed videos, substantially improving over prompt-only baselines with similarity score of 0.6, and supports multiple controlled variations that preserve the target's structure. Additional experiments show that augmenting prior image PSAs with inversion-derived inputs also improves reconstruction. Our results show that evaluations restricted to prompt recovery can underestimate an attacker's ability to reconstruct public generative outputs.
item.dc:creator: Junyan Huang, Sanskar Agmain, Chen Gong, Yan Pang, FNU Suya

item.title: Dissecting the GPU Load/Store Unit and Exposing Its Security Risks
item.description: arXiv:2611.23022v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: GPUs are the main platform for large-scale machine learning and power the largest supercomputers. Their load/store units (LSUs) often determine kernel performance and have been exploited in prior attacks. Yet what is known about the LSU is only a few isolated mechanisms and parameters, and even a single one has been enough for an attack. In particular, it is still unknown what a load costs, where loads contend, and even whether a warp can starve due to contention. Until each is measured, neither its security risk nor a defense is known. We reverse-engineer how the LSU serves load instructions on recent NVIDIA GPUs with microbenchmarks and analyze the security implications. We give a cycle-accurate latency formula for a global L1 hit or shared memory access from the addresses it touches, whose address-dependent terms are bank conflicts and the L1 tag lookup; we show that loads contend at both, and that when the LSU pipeline is full a warp can starve a warp of a later-launched block. We then show that the LSU's attack surface is far broader than prior attacks revealed: through channels never exploited before, it can leak information, communicate covertly, and degrade colocated workloads. Through either global bank conflicts or tag lookups alone, we recover a full AES-128 key under the threat model of prior GPU AES timing attacks. Under NVIDIA's Multi-Process Service (MPS), the bank access and the tag lookup each open a covert channel across processes, whose rate rises with each GPU generation. Also under MPS, this starvation lets one warp slow a colocated cuBLAS matrix multiplication by up to 750x on the A100 and 563x on the H100.
item.dc:creator: Wenbo Han, Pierre Talbot
